newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil says USDA coffee figure ignores crop cycles.
newsitem.headline: Brazil says USDA coffee figure ignores crop cycles.

text.p: An estimate by U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) pegging Brazil's 1997/98 coffee harvest at 28 million bags was not supported by a credible methodology and runs counter to crop cycles, a senior Brazilian official said.

"The analysis (of the figures)...does not reflect the natural tendency of Brazilian coffee production which is always subject to a bi-annual cycle," Mauricio Assis, head of the primary commodities department at the Industry and Commerce Ministry said in a statement.
The USDA report published Friday forecast that Brazil's production would rise from an estimated 27.5 million bags in 1996/97. Assis earlier this week called the forecast "absurd".
The Brazilian government believes that according to the bi-annual cycle in which high crops alternate with lower ones, Brazil should produce a smaller crop this year than last year.
It is working with a 1997/98 crop estimate of 22 million bags against 25 to 26 million bags in 1996/97.
Assis said the USDA should have explained how it reached its figure.

"Any forecast should be accompanied by the technical methodology and criteria used for evaluating the results, in order to confer credibility to the information, a fundamental condition which was not observed," he said.

USDA Tuesday defended the forecast, saying the high number reflected a number of factors including generally good growing conditions, an increased number of bearing trees and sharply higher prices than a year ago.
Assis said coffee production would drop sharply in the states of Minas Gerais and Espirito Santo this year, improve significantly in Parana and remain roughly the same in Sao Paulo.
"As can be seen, in most producing areas the low-production cycle is occurring...conferring credibility to the (ministry's) estimate of 21 to 22 million bags for 1997/98," he said.
